before.setup: I just really don't think that I am actually a morning person.
before.punchline: Basically I only kind of wake up when the coffee kicks in.

after.setup: I'm not a morning person.
after.punchline: I'm a coffee-has-kicked-in person.

note: Cut 'just', 'really', 'actually', 'basically', 'kind of'. 23 words became 10 and nothing was lost.

before.setup: So my dog is honestly just very, very lazy.
before.punchline: He literally sleeps for like twenty hours a day.

after.setup: My dog sleeps twenty hours a day.
after.punchline: And he still wakes up looking tired.

note: 'So', 'honestly', 'just', 'very, very', 'literally', 'like' were stalling. Laziness is shown by the twenty hours, so the word 'lazy' can go too.

before.setup: I basically went to the gym, like, three times this week.
before.punchline: And I actually only went inside once, just to use the bathroom.

after.setup: I went to the gym three times this week.
after.punchline: Once for the bathroom. Twice for the parking.

note: Hedges make you sound unsure the joke is worth telling. Remove them and the rhythm appears.

before.setup: You know how airports are really, really expensive?
before.punchline: I literally paid nine dollars for a bottle of water, I swear.

after.setup: Airport security took my water.
after.punchline: Then sold it back to me for nine dollars, twenty feet later.

note: 'I swear' and 'literally' ask the audience to believe you. A specific detail (twenty feet) does that job silently.

before.setup: My boss says we're like a family here.
before.punchline: Sure, the kind that doesn't talk at Thanksgiving, you know, at all.

after.setup: My boss says we're like a family here.
after.punchline: Sure. The kind that doesn't talk at Thanksgiving.

note: The laugh lives on 'Thanksgiving'. Every word after it ('you know, at all') steps on the laugh.

before.setup: I bought a smart fridge.
before.punchline: It tracks how often I open it and now it judges me for it.

after.setup: I bought a smart fridge.
after.punchline: It tracks how often I open it. Now I'm being judged by an appliance.

note: Ending on 'it' wastes the last beat. End on the image that is funny: being judged by an appliance.

before.setup: My cat left a dead mouse on my pillow.
before.punchline: I'm pretty sure it's a threat, so I've been extra nice to her lately.

after.setup: My cat left a dead mouse on my pillow.
after.punchline: That's not a gift. That's a horse head.

note: Find the one image that carries the joke (a mafia horse head) and make it the final two words.

before.setup: I asked my speaker to play something relaxing.
before.punchline: And then it went and turned off the news for me.

after.setup: I asked my speaker to play something relaxing.
after.punchline: It turned off the news.

note: 'For me' is a weak ending. 'News' is the surprise, so it goes last.

before.setup: I finally tried therapy.
before.punchline: My therapist fell asleep, forty minutes into the session.

after.setup: I finally tried therapy.
after.punchline: Forty minutes in, my therapist fell asleep.

note: Same words, reordered. The twist ('fell asleep') moved from the middle to the end.

before.setup: My dad just learned emojis.
before.punchline: A thumbs-up is how he ended the text that said Grandma's in hospital.

after.setup: My dad just learned emojis.
after.punchline: He texted me, "Grandma's in hospital." Thumbs-up.

note: The surprising word was the first word. Put the context first and the shock last.

before.setup: I joined a gym in January.
before.punchline: Forty dollars a month is what I've lost so far.

after.setup: I joined a gym in January.
after.punchline: So far I've lost forty dollars a month.

note: 'Lost' sets up weight loss; 'forty dollars a month' pays it off, so it has to be last.

before.setup: The doctor said I need eight hours of sleep.
before.punchline: In a row, I asked, and he didn't laugh.

after.setup: The doctor said I need eight hours of sleep.
after.punchline: I said, "In a row?"

note: Cut the after-the-laugh commentary and end on the twist itself.

before.setup: So the other day I was at the big supermarket near my house, in the queue for the self-checkout, which is always broken.
before.punchline: It said "unexpected item in bagging area." It was my self-esteem.

after.setup: The self-checkout said "unexpected item in bagging area."
after.punchline: It was my self-esteem.

note: The audience needs one fact to get the joke: what the machine said. 24 setup words became 8.

before.setup: My mom, who is sixty-two and lives in Ohio and recently got her very first smartphone, has started texting me.
before.punchline: Every text is CALL ME NOW and it's always about fruit.

after.setup: My mom texts like she's defusing a bomb.
after.punchline: "CALL ME NOW." I call. She wants to know if I'm eating fruit.

note: Biography is not setup. Keep only what the punchline needs: urgency.

before.setup: I've been trying to get healthier this year, so after a lot of research I decided to buy an expensive foam roller for my back.
before.punchline: Now I have a bad back and a very expensive pool noodle.

after.setup: I bought a foam roller to fix my back.
after.punchline: Now I have a bad back and a very expensive pool noodle.

note: Same punchline, half the setup. The faster you get there, the bigger the laugh.

before.setup: When I was younger, maybe twelve or thirteen, my parents made me take a nap every single afternoon and I hated it.
before.punchline: Now I'd pay for one.

after.setup: As a kid, I fought every nap.
after.punchline: Now I'd pay for one.

note: Short punchlines need short setups. Seven words do the work of twenty-two.

before.setup: My dog greets me like I've come home from war.
before.punchline: And the funny thing is that I actually only went outside to get the mail from the box at the end of the driveway.

after.setup: My dog greets me like I've come home from war.
after.punchline: I went to get the mail.

note: Never say 'the funny thing is'. The twist fits in six words.

before.setup: I have forty-seven unread emails.
before.punchline: Which, if you think about it, isn't really an inbox so much as a list of things to do that was written by people I've never met.

after.setup: I have forty-seven unread emails.
after.punchline: That's not an inbox. That's a to-do list written by strangers.

note: 'If you think about it' asks the audience to do your work. 'People I've never met' became 'strangers'.

before.setup: My phone is at two percent.
before.punchline: And this is always the exact moment when I suddenly become the most productive and focused person I have ever been.

after.setup: My phone is at two percent.
after.punchline: I've never been more productive, focused or afraid.

note: Shorter, and a third item ('afraid') turns the list into a joke.

before.setup: My bank sent me a yearly spending summary.
before.punchline: It read less like a summary and more like what your family reads to you at an intervention.

after.setup: My bank sent me a yearly spending summary.
after.punchline: It wasn't a summary. It was an intervention.

note: 'X? No, Y.' is a compact form. The punch word lands on its own.

before.setup: My cat acts like my manager by sitting on my laptop when I work.
before.punchline: She's not affectionate, she's management.

after.setup: My cat ignores me all day, then sits on my laptop the second I start working.
after.punchline: She's not affectionate. She's management.

note: The setup said 'manager', so the punchline had nothing left to surprise. Describe the behaviour and let the twist name it.

before.setup: My robot vacuum is as lost in life as I was in my twenties.
before.punchline: It hit the same wall eight times.

after.setup: I watched my robot vacuum hit the same wall eight times.
after.punchline: Finally, someone in this house who understands my twenties.

note: The comparison is the twist. It moved from the setup to the end.

before.setup: Airport security runs a water scam.
before.punchline: They took my water, then sold it back for six dollars.

after.setup: Airport security confiscated my water.
after.punchline: Then sold it back to me for six dollars. That's not security, that's a business model.

note: 'Scam' gave away the angle. A neutral setup makes the audience assume the normal story.

before.setup: Nobody listens to me except my smart speaker.
before.punchline: It listens to everything I say.

after.setup: My smart speaker listens to everything I say.
after.punchline: Joke's on them. Nobody else does.

note: Swapping the lines turns a sad statement into a reveal.

before.setup: My mom keeps a lot of stuff in a drawer.
before.punchline: It's a whole thing.

after.setup: My mom keeps plastic bags in a plastic bag,
after.punchline: inside a drawer of plastic bags. That's not storage. That's a nesting doll of fear.

note: 'Stuff' and 'thing' can't be pictured. Plastic bags in plastic bags can.

before.setup: I bought something to help my back.
before.punchline: Now I have a bad back and an expensive thing.

after.setup: I bought a foam roller to fix my back.
after.punchline: Now I have a bad back and a very expensive pool noodle.

note: Name the object, then name what it really is. 'Pool noodle' is funny; 'thing' is not.

before.setup: Some guy at the gym makes weird noises.
before.punchline: It's like he's going through something.

after.setup: The guy next to me grunts on every rep,
after.punchline: like he's lifting the weight and his entire childhood.

note: 'Weird noises' became 'grunts on every rep'; 'something' became 'his entire childhood'.

before.setup: My dad gives directions using places that aren't there anymore.
before.punchline: It's really confusing for people.

after.setup: My dad gives directions using landmarks that closed in 1994.
after.punchline: "Turn left where the video store used to be." Dad, it used to be everywhere.

note: A year, a quote and a specific shop. Specific details give the audience something to picture.

before.setup: My new apartment has everything I need:
before.punchline: a kitchen and a bathroom.

after.setup: My new apartment has everything I need:
after.punchline: a kitchen, a bathroom and a smell that doesn't pay rent.

note: Two items set a pattern and a third breaks it. Two items alone are only a list.

before.setup: I've tried yoga, pilates, spin class and running.
before.punchline: None of them stuck.

after.setup: I've tried yoga, pilates and lying on the floor near a yoga mat.
after.punchline: One of them stuck.

note: Four sincere items became two normal ones plus one wrong one.

before.setup: My ideal weekend is sleeping in, a long brunch, a walk in the park, and a nap.
before.punchline: Very relaxing.

after.setup: My ideal weekend: sleep in, long brunch,
after.punchline: and cancelling plans I made while I was confident.

note: The third item is the punchline, so make it the strange one.

before.setup: A good partner should be kind and patient.
before.punchline: And good at finding the remote.

after.setup: A good partner is kind, patient,
after.punchline: and can find the remote without asking where I "last had it."

note: Keep the rhythm in a single sentence (A, B, and twisted C) so the third item hits on the beat.

before.punchline: I hate when bosses say we're like a family since nobody talks at lunch and someone's always crying in the bathroom.

after.setup: My boss says we're like a family here.
after.punchline: Nobody talks at lunch and someone's always crying in the bathroom.

note: A joke has two halves: the expectation, then the turn. Split it where the turn starts.

before.punchline: Recipe blogs are annoying because I just want lasagna and now I know about your divorce.

after.setup: Recipe blogs make you read a life story before the ingredients.
after.punchline: I just wanted lasagna. Why do I know about your divorce?

note: 'Because' explains the joke. Put the complaint in the setup and the surprise in the punchline.

before.punchline: My phone told me my screen time went up and the funny part is I read it on my phone.

after.setup: My phone told me my screen time went up thirty percent.
after.punchline: Thanks. I read that on my phone.

note: Setup: the fact. Punchline: the irony, said as short as possible.

before.punchline: Doctors say you need eight hours of sleep and I always ask if they mean in a row.

after.setup: The doctor said I need eight hours of sleep.
after.punchline: I said, "In a row?"

note: Make it one specific moment instead of a habit ('always'). A scene is funnier than a generalisation.
